common_name: NC-4 Pecan (Northern Breeding Selection, Parent of Seneca)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter while dormant. A northern-origin breeding selection grown mainly in collections rather than commercial orchards; pair with a cultivar of opposite pollen-shed type if nut production is desired. Space 50-60 feet apart for full-sized trees.

directions: NC-4 is a named northern-origin pecan breeding selection derived from a cross of the classic native cultivars Colby and Peruque, developed as part of cold-hardy pecan improvement work for growers well outside the traditional Gulf South range. It is known chiefly for its role as a parent: in 1997 it was crossed with the companion selection NC-2B to produce the USDA Agricultural Research Service's pecan Seneca, patented for its compact habit, late spring bud break, and early fall dormancy. Little independent description of NC-4's own nut size, kernel percentage, or disease resistance has circulated outside breeding records, so it is best regarded as a historically significant breeding-line parent rather than a commercially offered orchard cultivar. Given its Colby and Peruque parentage, expect the strong cold hardiness typical of far-northern pecan selections.

common_name: NC-2B Pecan (Northern Breeding Selection, Parent of Seneca)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter while dormant. A northern-origin breeding selection grown mainly in collections rather than commercial orchards; pair with a cultivar of opposite pollen-shed type if nut production is desired. Space 50-60 feet apart for full-sized trees.

directions: NC-2B is the companion northern-origin pecan selection to NC-4, likewise derived from the classic native cultivars Colby and Peruque, and developed through cold-hardy pecan breeding work aimed at regions beyond the traditional Gulf South pecan belt. Its primary legacy is as a parent: crossed with NC-4 in 1997, the pairing produced the USDA Agricultural Research Service's Seneca pecan, patented for its compact size, late spring bud break, and early fall dormancy that give it strong freeze tolerance. Like NC-4, it is known mainly from breeding records rather than as a commercially available named cultivar, so specific nut size, kernel percentage, and scab resistance data have not been widely published for it on its own. It survives today chiefly in Northern Nut Growers Association literature discussing Seneca's parentage.
